bank.title: Rheumatology and Renal, set 1
bank.description: General practice rheumatology (inflammatory arthritis, crystal arthritis, PMR, osteoporosis, connective tissue disease) and kidney health (CKD, diabetes in CKD, haematuria, UTI, sick-day medicines). Adult only.

RACGP Curriculum and Syllabus, 6th edition (Musculoskeletal; Kidney and urinary health)

questions.source: CDNA Ross River virus infection surveillance case definition (2016); Australian Journal of General Practice: Paired serology for Ross River virus and Barmah Forest virus diseases (2019). TG not directly checked
stem: Hannah Price, 36, presents with 4 days of painful swelling of both wrists, several metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints and both ankles. She has also had a low-grade fever, myalgia and a faint maculopapular rash on her trunk. Ten days ago she returned from a camping trip along the Murray River near Mildura, where she had many mosquito bites. She has no past medical history and takes no regular medicines.

On examination, her temperature is 37.8 °C, with tender synovitis of both wrists and the 2nd and 3rd MCP joints bilaterally. You suspect Ross River virus infection. You request serology today and plan a second sample in 2 weeks.
questions.lead: Which result pattern would MOST reliably confirm recent Ross River virus infection?

options.text: Barmah Forest virus IgM and Ross River virus IgM both positive on the first sample
options.why: Dual IgM positivity on one sample usually reflects a false-positive or non-specific IgM, so it can't tell you which virus caused the illness or whether the infection is recent.

options.text: Rheumatoid factor positive at low titre, with negative anti-CCP antibodies
options.why: RF can be transiently positive after viral infections, so an early low-titre RF neither confirms RRV nor diagnoses RA. It does not test for RRV at all.

options.text: Ross River virus IgG negative on the first sample and positive on the second sample
options.why: IgG seroconversion between paired samples taken at least 2 weeks apart is laboratory definitive evidence of recent infection in the national case definition. IgM usually appears from about day 4 and IgG within about 2 weeks after it.

options.text: Ross River virus IgG positive at the same titre on both samples
options.why: A stable IgG titre means past infection. Prior RRV exposure is common in endemic areas.

options.text: Ross River virus IgM positive on both samples, with IgG negative on both samples
options.why: Common trap: IgG normally appears within about 2 weeks of IgM, so IgM without IgG seroconversion on paired samples suggests a false-positive or persistent non-specific IgM. IgM can also persist for months to years after past infection. This pattern does not confirm recent infection.

options.text: Ross River virus IgM positive, with a raised C-reactive protein
options.why: CRP is non-specific and adds nothing to the specificity of a single IgM result.

questions.keyPoint: Recent Ross River virus infection is confirmed by IgG seroconversion or a significant IgG rise on paired samples at least 2 weeks apart. A single positive IgM is not confirmatory. Treatment is supportive, mainly NSAIDs.

questions.source: EULAR recommendations for calcium pyrophosphate deposition, Part II: management (Ann Rheum Dis 2011). TG not directly checked
stem: Dorothy Whitfield, 79, presents with 2 days of a hot, swollen right knee. She can bear weight only with difficulty. Her past history includes type 2 diabetes, heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, chronic kidney disease, and a bleeding duodenal ulcer 2 years ago. Her medicines are metformin XR 1 g daily, linagliptin 5 mg daily, sacubitril/valsartan, bisoprolol, frusemide 40 mg daily and pantoprazole 40 mg daily.
On examination, her temperature is 37.6 °C and heart rate 78 bpm. There is a warm, tense right knee effusion. You aspirate the knee. A knee X-ray shows linear calcification of both menisci.
questions.lead: What is the MOST appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Allopurinol 50 mg orally, daily
options.why: Urate-lowering therapy is for gout. These are calcium pyrophosphate crystals (pseudogout), so it's the right drug for the wrong diagnosis.

options.text: Colchicine 1 mg orally, then 0.5 mg 1 hour later
options.why: Low-dose colchicine can treat acute CPP arthritis, but at 79 with an eGFR of 38 it needs a reduced dose and carries a higher toxicity risk. With a single joint that has just been aspirated, injection is more effective and safer.

options.text: Flucloxacillin 2 g intravenously, 6-hourly
options.why: A negative Gram stain, crystals, a WCC of 18 000 and low-grade fever fit crystal arthritis. Culture is pending, but suspicion of sepsis is not high enough to justify empirical IV antibiotics.

options.text: Indometacin 50 mg orally, 3 times daily
options.why: NSAIDs are unsafe here because of HFrEF, CKD and the previous bleeding ulcer.

options.text: Intra-articular corticosteroid injection into the right knee
options.why: EULAR recommends joint aspiration plus intra-articular corticosteroid as first-line treatment for acute CPP arthritis in one joint. It also avoids NSAID and colchicine risks and the systemic steroid effects on her poorly controlled diabetes and fluid balance. With crystals, a negative Gram stain and low clinical suspicion of sepsis, injecting before culture returns is reasonable. Safety-net: review the culture result, and return if fever develops or pain worsens.

options.text: Prednisolone 25 mg orally, daily until symptoms settle
options.why: Often chosen, and a reasonable fallback if injection isn't possible. With an HbA1c of 9.4% and heart failure, though, systemic steroid will worsen hyperglycaemia and fluid retention when a local option exists.

options.text: Probenecid 250 mg orally, twice daily
options.why: This is a uricosuric for chronic gout and has no role in CPPD.

options.text: Referral for arthroscopic washout
options.why: Washout is a treatment for septic arthritis, which this is not.

questions.keyPoint: Chondrocalcinosis plus positively birefringent rhomboid crystals means CPPD. For acute CPP arthritis in one joint, aspiration and intra-articular corticosteroid is first line, and it is the clear choice when NSAIDs and colchicine are risky.

questions.source: ACR Guideline for the Management of Gout (2020); CPIC guideline for HLA-B genotype and allopurinol dosing (2015 update); Australian Journal of General Practice: Allopurinol for gout, limited HLA-B*5801 screening (2022). TG not directly checked
stem: Wei Zhang, 54, of Han Chinese descent, attends to discuss urate-lowering therapy. He has had 3 gout flares in the past 12 months, and monosodium urate crystals were confirmed on aspiration of his left knee in March. His past history includes hypertension and chronic kidney disease, and he takes amlodipine 10 mg daily and irbesartan 300 mg daily. He currently has no symptoms.
questions.lead: Which investigation is MOST appropriate before starting allopurinol?

options.text: 24-hour urinary urate excretion
options.why: Not routinely needed. It can guide uricosuric choice but does not address the main risk of starting allopurinol in this patient.

options.text: Dual-energy CT of the feet
options.why: DECT is a specialist tool for diagnostically difficult cases. His gout is already crystal-proven.

options.text: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) activity
options.why: Relevant before rasburicase, dapsone or primaquine, not allopurinol. Right idea (pharmacogenomic screening), wrong drug.

options.text: HLA-B*1502
options.why: Common trap: HLA-B*1502 predicts carbamazepine-induced SJS/TEN in the same population. Right population, wrong drug.

options.text: HLA-B*5801
options.why: HLA-B*5801 is common in people of Han Chinese, Korean and Thai descent and strongly predicts allopurinol hypersensitivity syndrome (DRESS, SJS/TEN). ACR and CPIC advise testing before allopurinol in these groups, and CKD further raises the risk. If positive, avoid allopurinol and use probenecid or febuxostat (avoid febuxostat where possible in established cardiovascular disease). If negative, start low (50 mg daily with his eGFR) and titrate to target with colchicine flare prophylaxis.

options.text: HLA-B27
options.why: Associated with spondyloarthritis. It has no role in gout or allopurinol safety.

options.text: Thiopurine methyltransferase (TPMT) activity
options.why: Used before azathioprine or mercaptopurine. Allopurinol does interact with those drugs, but TPMT says nothing about allopurinol risk.

questions.keyPoint: Before allopurinol in people of Han Chinese, Korean or Thai descent, especially with CKD, check HLA-B*5801. Start low, go slow, use flare prophylaxis, and treat to a urate below 0.36 mmol/L.

questions.source: RACGP and Healthy Bones Australia guideline for osteoporosis management and fracture prevention in postmenopausal women and men over 50 years of age (2024)
stem: Rosa Mancini, 76, has had denosumab 60 mg subcutaneously every 6 months for 7 years, started after a minimal-trauma T12 vertebral fracture. Her last injection was 6 months ago and the next is due this week. After reading about osteonecrosis of the jaw she wants to stop. You have discussed the risks of stopping and she has made an informed decision. She has had no further fractures.
questions.lead: What is the MOST appropriate plan?

options.text: Alendronate 70 mg orally weekly, starting now and continuing for 12–24 months
options.why: Stopping denosumab causes rebound bone turnover and multiple spontaneous vertebral fractures, a risk highest in those with a previous vertebral fracture. The RACGP and Healthy Bones Australia guideline says denosumab should not be interrupted, and if it is stopped the patient should move to a bisphosphonate for at least 12 months. Start when the next denosumab dose would have been due, which is now. Counsel that alendronate also carries a small MRONJ risk.

options.text: Calcium and vitamin D supplements alone, with DXA in 2 years
options.why: Unsafe: Without a replacement antiresorptive, bone loss is rapid and fracture risk rebounds within months.

options.text: Denosumab 60 mg once yearly instead of 6-monthly
options.why: Rebound turnover starts about 7 months after the last dose, and delays of more than 4 months are linked to rebound vertebral fractures. Denosumab is not dosed yearly.

options.text: Drug holiday for 12 months, then repeat DXA
options.why: Common trap: Drug holidays apply to bisphosphonates, which have a long skeletal half-life. Denosumab's effect wears off once it is stopped.

options.text: Raloxifene 60 mg orally daily
options.why: Raloxifene is weaker, not shown to prevent post-denosumab rebound, and carries VTE risk at 76.

options.text: Teriparatide 20 micrograms subcutaneously daily for 18 months
options.why: She doesn't meet the PBS criteria. Moving from denosumab straight to an anabolic causes transient bone loss, so it is not a transition strategy.

options.text: Zoledronic acid 5 mg intravenously, 12 months after the last denosumab dose
options.why: Zoledronic acid can be a transition agent, but at 12 months the 6-month gap means rebound turnover is already under way.

questions.keyPoint: Denosumab must be continued or replaced by a bisphosphonate for at least 12 months, started when the next dose is due. Never leave a gap.

questions.source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology (polymyalgia rheumatica); EULAR/ACR recommendations for the management of polymyalgia rheumatica (2015); Australian Prescriber: Prescribing for polymyalgia rheumatica (2018)
stem: Graham Ellis, 71, was diagnosed with polymyalgia rheumatica 8 months ago. He responded promptly to prednisolone 15 mg daily and has followed a taper; 3 weeks ago his dose went from 8 mg to 7 mg daily.

For the past 10 days he has had recurrent bilateral shoulder and hip-girdle pain, with 90 minutes of morning stiffness. He has no headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, visual symptoms, fever or weight loss.
questions.lead: What is the MOST appropriate change to his corticosteroid therapy?

options.text: Continue prednisolone 7 mg daily and reassure him that symptoms are expected during tapering
options.why: Common trap: Mild aching for a few days after a dose reduction can be watched, with the plan continued. Ten days of recurrent girdle pain and stiffness with a clear rise in ESR and CRP meets the definition of relapse, though, and needs a dose increase.

options.text: Increase prednisolone to 8 mg daily, then reduce back to 7 mg over 4–8 weeks
options.why: For relapse, EULAR/ACR advise returning to the pre-relapse dose (here 8 mg), then reducing over 4–8 weeks to the dose at which relapse occurred. Also check again for GCA features. Consider specialist referral if relapses recur, as methotrexate is the usual steroid-sparing option.

options.text: Increase prednisolone to 10 mg daily, then reduce by 1 mg every 4 weeks
options.why: The right idea at the wrong dose. It gives more steroid than needed and adds cumulative harm.

options.text: Increase prednisolone to 15 mg daily and restart the original taper
options.why: Overtreats a mild relapse and adds months of avoidable steroid exposure.

options.text: Increase prednisolone to 60 mg daily
options.why: This is a GCA starting dose (40–60 mg daily). He has no headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication or visual symptoms.

options.text: Methylprednisolone 500 mg intravenously daily for 3 days
options.why: Pulse IV methylprednisolone is reserved for GCA with evolving or recent transient visual loss.

options.text: Stop prednisolone and start methotrexate 10 mg weekly
options.why: Stopping abruptly after 8 months risks adrenal crisis and relapse. Methotrexate is a specialist-initiated steroid-sparing add-on, not a replacement.

questions.keyPoint: PMR relapse means recurrent symptoms with a rise in inflammatory markers. Go back to the last dose that controlled it, not the starting dose, then reduce over 4–8 weeks. Refer if relapses recur, the dose can't be tapered, or steroids are still needed after 2 years.

questions.source: Kidney Health Australia, CKD Management in Primary Care, 5th edition
stem: Leanne Fraser, 61, has had type 2 diabetes for 12 years and also has hypertension. Her medicines are perindopril 10 mg daily (maximum dose, for 2 years), amlodipine 5 mg daily, metformin XR 1 g twice daily and atorvastatin 40 mg daily. Her blood pressure is 126/74 mmHg.
questions.lead: Which medicine is the MOST appropriate addition to slow progression of her kidney disease?

options.text: Dapagliflozin 10 mg orally, daily
options.why: Kidney Health Australia's stepwise plan for persistent albuminuria is: maximise the ACE inhibitor or ARB, add an SGLT2 inhibitor, then (in type 2 diabetes) consider a non-steroidal MRA and a GLP-1 RA. Expect a reversible eGFR dip, consider diuretic or antihypertensive reduction, and give sick-day advice. Her persistent UACR above 30 also meets a nephrology referral criterion.

options.text: Finerenone 10 mg orally, daily
options.why: Common trap: Finerenone fits her profile (type 2 diabetes, albuminuria, K⁺ ≤ 5.0), but in the stepwise sequence it comes after the SGLT2 inhibitor.

options.text: Frusemide 20 mg orally, daily
options.why: No renoprotective effect, and she has no oedema.

options.text: Irbesartan 150 mg orally, daily
options.why: Combining an ACE inhibitor with an ARB isn't recommended because of hyperkalaemia and AKI risk without outcome benefit.

options.text: Semaglutide 0.25 mg subcutaneously, weekly
options.why: A GLP-1 RA is a later step, considered once SGLT2 inhibitor therapy is in place.

options.text: Sitagliptin 100 mg orally, daily
options.why: Glucose-lowering only, with no kidney benefit, and her HbA1c is near target.

options.text: Spironolactone 25 mg orally, daily
options.why: A steroidal MRA on top of an ACE inhibitor in CKD carries a high hyperkalaemia risk. It is used for heart failure or resistant hypertension, not to reduce albuminuria.

questions.keyPoint: For albuminuric CKD: ACE inhibitor or ARB at maximum dose, then SGLT2 inhibitor, then finerenone or a GLP-1 RA in type 2 diabetes. Aim for at least a 30% fall in UACR.

questions.source: Kidney Health Australia, CKD Management in Primary Care, 5th edition (2024); Australian Diabetes Society, Australian Type 2 Diabetes Glycaemic Management Algorithm (2024); Trajenta (linagliptin) product information (2024)
stem: Beatrice Holloway, 78, lives alone and has type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease. Her medicines are metformin XR 1 g daily, gliclazide MR 30 mg daily, dapagliflozin 10 mg daily, perindopril 5 mg daily and atorvastatin 20 mg daily. She reports no hypoglycaemia.
questions.lead: What is the MOST appropriate change to her glucose-lowering therapy?

options.text: Cease metformin and start glibenclamide 5 mg daily
options.why: Glibenclamide has active, renally cleared metabolites and causes prolonged hypoglycaemia in CKD. Avoid it.

options.text: Cease metformin and start linagliptin 5 mg daily
options.why: Metformin is contraindicated below an eGFR of 30 because of lactic acidosis risk. Linagliptin is cleared hepatobiliary and needs no dose change in CKD, so it suits her. It doesn't cause hypoglycaemia on its own but adds to the risk from gliclazide, so monitor her glucose and stop gliclazide if hypoglycaemia occurs. Continue dapagliflozin for kidney protection.

options.text: Cease metformin and start saxagliptin 5 mg daily
options.why: The right class at the wrong dose. Saxagliptin is reduced to 2.5 mg daily in moderate to severe kidney impairment.

options.text: Cease metformin and start sitagliptin 100 mg daily
options.why: The right class at the wrong dose. Sitagliptin is 25 mg daily when the eGFR is below 30.

options.text: Continue the current regimen
options.why: Metformin at an eGFR of 26 is unsafe.

options.text: Increase gliclazide MR to 120 mg daily
options.why: Raises hypoglycaemia risk in a 78-year-old with CKD who lives alone, and doesn't deal with the metformin.

options.text: Reduce metformin XR to 500 mg daily
options.why: Often chosen because it misapplies the eGFR 30–44 rule (maximum 1 g daily). Below 30, metformin should be stopped, not reduced.

questions.keyPoint: Metformin: maximum 1 g daily at eGFR 30–44, stop below 30. Of the gliptins, only linagliptin needs no renal dose adjustment.

questions.source: Kidney Health Australia, CKD Management in Primary Care, 5th edition (haematuria)
stem: Ian Moretti, 66, a retired panel beater, reports one episode of painless red urine with small clots 5 days ago, which cleared within a day. He has no dysuria, loin pain, fever or lower urinary tract symptoms. He has atrial fibrillation and takes apixaban 5 mg twice daily. He is an ex-smoker with 30 pack-years who quit 8 years ago.
Examination is unremarkable apart from a smooth, mildly enlarged prostate.
questions.lead: What is the MOST appropriate next step?

options.text: Cease apixaban and repeat urinalysis in 2 weeks
options.why: Stopping apixaban raises stroke risk and doesn't remove the need to investigate. Anticoagulation unmasks pathology rather than causing it.

options.text: CT urogram and referral to a urologist for cystoscopy
options.why: Even a single episode of visible haematuria needs full evaluation. His age, smoking history and solvent and paint exposure all raise urothelial cancer risk, and clots suggest a lower-tract source. CT urography images the upper tract and cystoscopy the bladder (RACGP syllabus). eGFR 76 means negligible contrast risk.

options.text: Plain X-ray of the kidneys, ureters and bladder
options.why: The RACGP syllabus states plain KUB X-ray has no role in investigating haematuria.

options.text: Prostate-specific antigen, with urology referral only if raised
options.why: PSA does not assess the urothelium or kidney, and a normal result would falsely reassure.

options.text: Referral to a nephrologist
options.why: Clots, no albuminuria and a normal eGFR point to a urological, non-glomerular source. Nephrology is the pathway for glomerular haematuria.

options.text: Repeat urinalysis in 3 months, attributing the bleeding to anticoagulation
options.why: Common trap: Haematuria on anticoagulants should be investigated exactly as it would be without them.

options.text: Urine cytology on 3 samples, with urology referral only if positive
options.why: Cytology has low sensitivity, so cystoscopy is indicated even when cytology is negative.

questions.keyPoint: Visible haematuria in an adult means CT urography plus cystoscopy, whatever the anticoagulation status.

questions.source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Acute cystitis in adults (2025)
stem: Robert Sutherland, 58, presents with 2 days of dysuria, frequency and urgency. He has no fever, rigors, loin or perineal pain, difficulty passing urine or urethral discharge. He is in a long-term monogamous relationship, has had no recent antibiotics or hospital admissions, and takes no regular medicines.
His temperature is 37.1 °C, there is no renal angle tenderness, and on digital rectal examination the prostate is normal-sized and non-tender. You send a midstream urine sample for culture.
questions.lead: What is the MOST appropriate empirical antibiotic regimen while awaiting culture?

options.text: Amoxicillin+clavulanate 875+125 mg orally, 12-hourly for 10 days
options.why: Broader spectrum than needed. TG reserves amoxicillin+clavulanate (8-hourly) for empirical treatment of pyelonephritis.

options.text: Cefalexin 500 mg orally, 12-hourly for 7 days
options.why: TG lists this only if trimethoprim and nitrofurantoin can't be used.

options.text: Ciprofloxacin 500 mg orally, 12-hourly for 14 days
options.why: Fluoroquinolones are reserved to limit resistance. He has no features of prostatitis or pyelonephritis.

options.text: Doxycycline 100 mg orally, 12-hourly for 7 days
options.why: Treats chlamydial urethritis. With no discharge, low STI risk and a positive nitrite test, this is bacterial cystitis.

options.text: Fosfomycin 3 g orally, as a single dose
options.why: TG lists single-dose fosfomycin for non-pregnant women, not for men.

options.text: Nitrofurantoin 100 mg orally, 6-hourly for 5 days
options.why: Common trap: Nitrofurantoin is now the TG first-line drug for cystitis in men, but for 7 days. Five days is the course for non-pregnant women.

options.text: Trimethoprim 300 mg orally, daily for 3 days
options.why: Common trap: This is the regimen for non-pregnant women. Men need 7 days.

options.text: Trimethoprim 300 mg orally, daily for 7 days
options.why: The best of these options for cystitis in men when prostatitis is unlikely. Since 2025 TG lists nitrofurantoin 100 mg 6-hourly for 7 days first and trimethoprim second, because more than 20% of E. coli urine isolates are now resistant to trimethoprim, so check the culture result and change only if symptoms aren't improving on a resistant isolate. Cystitis in men often reflects a urinary tract abnormality, so refer to a urologist if symptoms persist after treatment.

questions.keyPoint: Male cystitis: send an MSU, then nitrofurantoin 100 mg 6-hourly (first line) or trimethoprim 300 mg daily, both for 7 days. Think prostatitis if there's fever, obstructive symptoms or a tender prostate, and don't use nitrofurantoin if it's possible.

questions.source: ACR/EULAR classification criteria for systemic sclerosis (2013); Australian Family Physician: Nailfold dermatoscopy in general practice (2015)
stem: Natalie Brooks, 44, an office manager, has had 5 months of fingers turning white, then blue, then red in the cold. She now has painful sores on two fingertips. She also reports worsening heartburn, and her fingers feel puffy and tight in the mornings. She has no rash, joint swelling, or dry eyes or mouth. She takes no regular medicines and has never smoked.

On examination there are healed pitting scars on two fingertips and mild skin thickening of the fingers distal to the MCP joints. Dermatoscopy shows dilated nailfold capillaries. Her blood pressure is 122/78 mmHg.
questions.lead: Which investigation is MOST useful to support the likely diagnosis?

options.text: Anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (anti-CCP) antibodies
options.why: A marker for RA, and she has no synovitis.

options.text: Anti-double-stranded DNA antibodies
options.why: Specific for SLE, but she has no SLE features, and ANA is the screening test either way.

options.text: Anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA)
options.why: Used for small-vessel vasculitis. Nothing here suggests vasculitis.

options.text: Antinuclear antibodies (ANA) with an extractable nuclear antigen (ENA) panel
options.why: Onset after 30, digital pitting scars, sclerodactyly, puffy fingers, reflux and abnormal nailfold capillaries all point to secondary Raynaud phenomenon from systemic sclerosis. ANA is positive in over 90%. The ENA panel and IIF pattern give the subtype: anti-centromere for limited, anti-Scl-70 for diffuse disease and lung involvement, anti-RNA polymerase III for renal crisis risk. Refer to rheumatology.

options.text: Creatine kinase
options.why: Only relevant if weakness suggests overlap myositis.

options.text: Cryoglobulins
options.why: Raynaud phenomenon can occur in cryoglobulinaemia, but there's no purpura, hepatitis C or vasculitic picture.

options.text: HLA-B27
options.why: Used for spondyloarthritis, which isn't relevant here.

options.text: Rheumatoid factor
options.why: Non-specific and positive in many connective tissue diseases, so it won't confirm systemic sclerosis.

questions.keyPoint: Secondary Raynaud phenomenon (late onset, digital pits or ulcers, abnormal capillaries) warrants ANA and ENA. In systemic sclerosis, monitor blood pressure and avoid high-dose steroids because of the risk of scleroderma renal crisis.

questions.source: Australian Immunisation Handbook (zoster and pneumococcal chapters, 2026); Australian Rheumatology Association: Methotrexate patient information (2024); Australian Prescriber: Managing the drug treatment of rheumatoid arthritis (2017); EULAR recommendations for infection screening in autoimmune inflammatory rheumatic diseases (2022)
stem: Ronald Pike, 71, a retired electrician, was diagnosed with seropositive rheumatoid arthritis by a rheumatologist last week, with synovitis in 8 joints. The rheumatologist has started prednisolone 10 mg daily as a bridge and plans methotrexate 15 mg weekly with folic acid in 2 weeks. Their letter asks you to complete the pre-treatment work-up and preventive care.

He has hypertension (amlodipine 5 mg daily). He drinks 2 standard drinks most nights, about 12 a week. He was born in Australia, has no TB risk factors and no respiratory symptoms, and has never had hepatitis serology. He had an influenza vaccine in April this year and a 21-valent pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (21vPCV) 2 months ago. He has never had a zoster vaccine.
questions.lead: Which FIVE actions are MOST appropriate before methotrexate starts?

options.text: Advise substantially reducing his alcohol intake while taking methotrexate
options.why: Alcohol adds to methotrexate liver toxicity. ARA advice is that 1 to 2 standard drinks once or twice a week is unlikely to cause harm, so 12 a week is too many.

options.text: Baseline full blood count, liver function tests, and urea, electrolytes and creatinine
options.why: Needed as a baseline for marrow, liver and kidney toxicity. Methotrexate is renally cleared, so dosing depends on the eGFR.

options.text: Chest X-ray
options.why: A baseline chest X-ray (if none in the past 12 months) is standard before methotrexate, for comparison if pneumonitis or RA lung disease develops later.

options.text: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) activity
options.why: Relevant for dapsone, primaquine or rasburicase. Not needed for methotrexate.

options.text: Hepatitis B and hepatitis C serology
options.why: Critical: Immunosuppression can reactivate hepatitis B, sometimes fatally, and chronic hepatitis B or C greatly increases methotrexate liver toxicity. Test HBsAg, anti-HBc and anti-HBs, and hepatitis C antibody.

options.text: HLA-B27
options.why: Used for spondyloarthritis. It has no place here.

options.text: Interferon-gamma release assay (QuantiFERON-TB)
options.why: Common trap: Before methotrexate, TB screening starts with a risk assessment, and he has no risk factors or symptoms. Routine IGRA is required before biological or targeted synthetic DMARDs, and is only considered before methotrexate when risk factors are present.

options.text: Measure varicella-zoster IgG before zoster vaccination
options.why: Serology is not recommended before or after zoster vaccination. Most adults have had chickenpox, and the recombinant vaccine is given regardless of the result.

options.text: Ophthalmology referral for baseline retinal screening
options.why: Retinal screening is for hydroxychloroquine, not methotrexate. The right test for the wrong drug.

options.text: Recombinant zoster vaccine, 2 doses
options.why: Being non-live, it is safe on immunosuppression and best started before methotrexate. It is the only zoster vaccine now available in Australia and is funded on the NIP from age 65. In immunocompromised people the 2 doses can be given 1–2 months apart.

options.text: Repeat 21-valent pneumococcal conjugate vaccine
options.why: He had his adult 21vPCV dose 2 months ago. An adult who has had it does not need another dose when a risk condition such as immunosuppressive therapy develops.

options.text: Repeat anti-CCP antibody titre
options.why: Antibody titres don't guide treatment or monitoring. This is low-value testing.

options.text: Thiopurine methyltransferase (TPMT) activity
options.why: Done before azathioprine, not methotrexate.

questions.keyPoint: Before methotrexate: bloods (FBC, LFT, EUC), hepatitis B and C serology, baseline chest X-ray, non-live vaccines (recombinant zoster) and alcohol advice. TB screening is by risk assessment, with routine IGRA kept for biologics. Retinal screening is for hydroxychloroquine.

questions.source: RACGP and Healthy Bones Australia guideline for osteoporosis management and fracture prevention in postmenopausal women and men over 50 years of age (2024); zoledronic acid (Aclasta) Australian product information
stem: Edna Kowalski, 83, who weighs 68 kg, attends 2 weeks after discharge from hospital, where her left intertrochanteric fracture was fixed after she tripped over a rug at home. She lives alone and has had 2 other falls in the past year. Her past history includes Barrett's oesophagus (pantoprazole 40 mg daily), hypertension (perindopril 5 mg daily) and knee osteoarthritis. She has about one glass of milk a day and rarely other dairy, giving an estimated calcium intake of 400 mg a day.
The discharge summary recommends zoledronic acid in general practice.
questions.lead: Which FOUR actions are MOST appropriate?

options.text: Advise paracetamol before the infusion and for several days afterwards
options.why: Paracetamol around the time of the infusion reduces the flu-like acute-phase reaction over the first 3 days, which is most common after the first infusion. Ibuprofen is the alternative in the product information but is a poor choice with her kidney function and perindopril.

options.text: Alendronate 70 mg orally weekly instead of zoledronic acid
options.why: Active upper GI disease such as Barrett's oesophagus is a reason to avoid oral bisphosphonates, which is why IV was recommended.

options.text: Bone turnover markers (serum CTX) before treatment
options.why: Not recommended routinely in general practice. Specialists may use them for monitoring.

options.text: Calcium carbonate supplement providing 1500 mg elemental calcium daily
options.why: The right idea at the wrong dose. The aim is a total intake of about 1300 mg a day, mainly from food, with a supplement only filling the gap (usually 500–600 mg). Adding 1500 mg to her 400 mg diet overshoots, and higher doses cause constipation and possibly add cardiovascular risk.

options.text: Cholecalciferol (vitamin D3) replacement, then recheck 25-hydroxyvitamin D before the infusion
options.why: Critical: Vitamin D should be above 50 nmol/L before starting antiresorptive therapy, and zoledronic acid is contraindicated in hypocalcaemia and needs a creatinine clearance of at least 35 mL/min and good hydration. Infusing at 31 nmol/L risks symptomatic hypocalcaemia. The mildly raised PTH is secondary to vitamin D deficiency.

options.text: Denosumab 60 mg subcutaneously today instead of zoledronic acid
options.why: Denosumab also needs vitamin D and calcium corrected first, and hypocalcaemia is more likely with reduced kidney function. It also commits her to uninterrupted 6-monthly dosing, with rebound vertebral fractures if a dose is late or it is stopped without a bisphosphonate.

options.text: Falls prevention: physiotherapy for strength and balance training, and an occupational therapy home safety assessment
options.why: She has recurrent falls and tripped at home. Strength and balance training and a home safety assessment reduce falls, and falls prevention is part of fracture prevention after a hip fracture.

options.text: Increase dietary calcium towards 1300 mg a day, adding a 500–600 mg supplement only if this can't be reached
options.why: The recommended intake on osteoporosis treatment is 1300 mg a day, ideally from food. A supplement fills any gap.

options.text: Reduce the zoledronic acid dose to 2.5 mg because of her eGFR
options.why: There is no dose reduction for zoledronic acid. It is contraindicated if creatinine clearance is below 35 mL/min (hers is about 39 mL/min by Cockcroft-Gault) and otherwise given as 5 mg over at least 15 minutes, with good hydration.

options.text: Refer for parathyroidectomy
options.why: Low-normal calcium with a raised PTH is secondary hyperparathyroidism from vitamin D deficiency, not primary disease.

options.text: Stop pantoprazole to reduce fracture risk
options.why: Barrett's oesophagus is a firm indication for the PPI. PPIs only modestly increase fracture risk.

options.text: Zoledronic acid 5 mg intravenously at today's visit
options.why: Often chosen because the hospital recommended it. It is unsafe until her vitamin D is replete.

questions.keyPoint: Before zoledronic acid: 25-OH vitamin D above 50 nmol/L, normal corrected calcium, creatinine clearance of at least 35 mL/min and good hydration. Give paracetamol cover, and don't forget calcium intake and falls prevention.

questions.source: Kidney Health Australia, CKD Management in Primary Care, 5th edition (sick day medicines)
stem: Theo Papadopoulos, 74, has had 3 days of watery diarrhoea after his grandchildren had gastroenteritis. His vomiting stopped yesterday. He is now keeping oral fluids down and passing urine, and he took ibuprofen 400 mg 3 times daily for 2 days for aches.

He has type 2 diabetes, hypertension and CKD G3a A2, with a baseline creatinine of 112 µmol/L (eGFR 54) 3 months ago. His medicines are perindopril/indapamide 10/2.5 mg daily, metformin XR 1 g twice daily, empagliflozin 10 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg daily and aspirin 100 mg daily.
On examination: temperature 37.2 °C, heart rate 96 bpm, lying blood pressure 114/70 mmHg (usually 134/80), dry mucous membranes, soft abdomen. He is alert. You advise oral rehydration solution.
questions.lead: Which FIVE further actions are MOST appropriate?

options.text: Arrange hospital admission for intravenous fluids
options.why: He is alert, keeping fluids down, passing urine and has mild hyperkalaemia, so outpatient care with close review is reasonable. Admit if he can't maintain fluids, creatinine rises further, K⁺ reaches 6.0 or more, or ketones rise.

options.text: Cease aspirin 100 mg
options.why: The 'triple whammy' caution excludes low-dose aspirin. Keep it for cardiovascular protection.

options.text: Cease atorvastatin
options.why: Statins aren't a sick-day medicine and don't cause prerenal AKI.

options.text: Cease ibuprofen
options.why: Critical: An NSAID with an ACE inhibitor and diuretic in a volume-depleted patient with CKD is the triple whammy, and the most modifiable cause of this AKI (creatinine 1.5 times baseline).

options.text: Commence gliclazide MR 30 mg daily while metformin is withheld
options.why: Sulfonylureas are themselves sick-day medicines because of hypoglycaemia with poor intake, and a glucose of 8.9 needs no cover.

options.text: Halve the dose of perindopril/indapamide and continue it
options.why: A half measure. During dehydration and AKI the ACE inhibitor and diuretic should be withheld entirely.

options.text: Permanently stop empagliflozin because of the AKI
options.why: Withhold it temporarily and restart once he is eating and drinking normally. Its long-term kidney and heart benefit still applies.

options.text: Repeat urea, electrolytes and creatinine within 24–48 hours
options.why: Confirms the AKI is recovering and the K⁺ is falling. Escalate if it isn't.

options.text: Request an urgent renal tract ultrasound
options.why: Low value. The cause is clearly prerenal, so ultrasound is only needed if kidney function doesn't recover.

options.text: Send stool for microscopy, culture and PCR
options.why: Short, resolving, household-acquired gastroenteritis is almost always viral, and the result won't change management.

options.text: Sodium polystyrene sulfonate for the potassium
options.why: A K⁺ of 5.3 will correct once the ACE inhibitor and NSAID are stopped and the AKI resolves.

options.text: Withhold empagliflozin
options.why: SGLT2 inhibitors are withheld when intake is poor because of volume depletion and euglycaemic ketoacidosis risk (his ketones of 0.3 are reassuring).

options.text: Withhold metformin
options.why: Withhold during dehydration and AKI because of lactic acidosis risk, especially now his eGFR is 33.

options.text: Withhold perindopril/indapamide
options.why: Both the ACE inhibitor and the diuretic worsen prerenal AKI and hyperkalaemia during volume depletion.

questions.keyPoint: Sick-day rules (SADMANS): sulfonylureas, ACE inhibitors, diuretics, metformin, ARBs, NSAIDs, SGLT2 inhibitors. Restart them once he has been eating and drinking normally for 24–48 hours, then recheck EUC.

stem: Marguerite Lam, 64, a retired teacher, has had 4 culture-confirmed episodes of E. coli cystitis in the past 12 months, each responding to trimethoprim. She has no symptoms at present. She went through menopause 12 years ago, is not on hormone therapy and reports vaginal dryness. She is not sexually active and drinks about 1.5 L of fluid a day.
A renal tract ultrasound and post-void residual volume are normal, and she has had no haematuria between infections. Her eGFR is 78. She would like to avoid long-term antibiotics.
questions.lead: Which TWO strategies are MOST appropriate to reduce her risk of recurrence?

options.text: Continuous trimethoprim 150 mg orally at night
options.why: Antibiotic prophylaxis works, but she wants to avoid long-term antibiotics and there are effective non-antibiotic options. It would be correct in another setting.

options.text: Cranberry products daily
options.why: Common trap: TG says cranberry may reduce recurrence only in non-pregnant women under 50, and evidence is insufficient in older women.

options.text: Cystoscopy referral
options.why: Not indicated: she has normal imaging, a normal residual volume and no haematuria.

options.text: Increase water intake by 1.5 L a day
options.why: TG evidence applies to premenopausal women drinking less than 1.5 L a day. She already drinks 1.5 L.

options.text: Intravaginal oestrogen (for example oestriol cream)
options.why: Critical: In postmenopausal women, vaginal oestrogen restores vaginal flora and reduces recurrent UTI. She also has atrophic symptoms.

options.text: Methenamine hippurate 1 g orally 12-hourly, reviewed every 6 months
options.why: TG: reduces recurrent UTI and is a reasonable alternative to continuous antibiotics in non-pregnant women.

options.text: Post-coital single-dose antibiotic
options.why: Only for infections linked to intercourse, and she is not sexually active.

options.text: Routine urine culture every 3 months while she has no symptoms
options.why: Treating asymptomatic bacteriuria causes harm. Culture only for symptoms.

options.text: Systemic menopausal hormone therapy
options.why: Systemic hormone therapy hasn't been shown to prevent UTI, and the benefit comes from vaginal oestrogen.

options.text: Urinary alkalinising agent daily
options.why: No preventive effect, and alkaline urine stops methenamine working (it needs acidic urine).

options.text: Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) 1 g daily
options.why: TG: ascorbic acid does not appear to prevent UTI.

questions.keyPoint: For recurrent UTI after menopause, use vaginal oestrogen first, then methenamine. Cranberry evidence applies only to women under 50.

questions.source: Kidney Health Australia, CKD Management in Primary Care, 5th edition (2024); KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Lupus Nephritis (2024); Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology
stem: Priya Nair, 29, was diagnosed with SLE 3 years ago (arthritis, malar rash, positive ANA and anti-dsDNA) and has been stable on hydroxychloroquine 200 mg twice daily. She weighs 82 kg. Her urinalysis at review 12 months ago was normal.

She now has 3 weeks of ankle swelling and frothy urine, with mild hand arthralgia. She is sexually active with a male partner and uses condoms inconsistently. Her last menstrual period was 3 weeks ago.
On examination her blood pressure is 154/98 mmHg (previously 116/72), with pitting oedema to mid-shin and no rash.

head: Test
Result
Reference
rows: Blood 3+, protein 3+, leucocytes and nitrites negative

questions.lead: Which THREE actions are MOST appropriate now?

options.text: 24-hour urine protein collection
options.why: Not needed: UACR quantifies the proteinuria, and the nephrologist will decide on further testing.

options.text: ANCA and anti-GBM antibodies
options.why: Low yield given active SLE serology (low complement, rising dsDNA). The specialist can add these if the biopsy is atypical.

options.text: Cease hydroxychloroquine
options.why: Continue it. Hydroxychloroquine reduces flares and improves kidney outcomes in lupus nephritis, and at 82 kg her dose is within 5 mg/kg.

options.text: Ibuprofen 400 mg 3 times daily for her arthralgia
options.why: NSAIDs worsen kidney function, blood pressure and oedema in active nephritis.

options.text: Increase hydroxychloroquine to 600 mg daily
options.why: This exceeds 5 mg/kg, raising retinal toxicity risk, and doesn't treat nephritis.

options.text: Prednisolone 1 mg/kg orally daily, starting today before specialist review
options.why: Common trap: Induction therapy is specialist-directed and ideally guided by biopsy. Starting high-dose steroid before that discussion is premature.

options.text: Pregnancy test and advice on effective contraception
options.why: Pregnancy with active lupus nephritis carries high risks (pre-eclampsia, pregnancy loss, flare), and likely treatments such as mycophenolate, cyclophosphamide and ACE inhibitors are teratogenic. Prefer progestogen-only methods or an IUD until antiphospholipid status is known.

options.text: Repeat UACR twice over the next 3 months to confirm persistence
options.why: Unsafe delay: That rule is for CKD screening. Acute nephritis is a medical emergency (Kidney Health Australia).

options.text: Routine rheumatology outpatient referral
options.why: The wrong urgency, and the wrong first port of call for nephritis.

options.text: Urgent nephrology referral, discussed by phone today
options.why: Critical: New severely increased albuminuria with haematuria, new hypertension, oedema, a rising creatinine, low complement and rising dsDNA mean lupus nephritis until proven otherwise. KHA: refer signs of acute nephritis without delay. A biopsy will decide induction therapy.

options.text: Urine cytology
options.why: Belongs to the urological malignancy pathway, not glomerular disease.

options.text: Urine microscopy for dysmorphic red cells and red cell casts
options.why: Confirms a glomerular source and is part of the KHA pre-referral work-up. Request it the same day without delaying referral.

questions.keyPoint: In SLE, new proteinuria, haematuria, hypertension or oedema means lupus nephritis until proven otherwise. Refer the same day, confirm a glomerular source, continue hydroxychloroquine, and sort out contraception.
